## Stage 2.5

### 2020-2025

Previously I analyzed 2025 data. To add a dimension for further analysis, I am expanding my dataset to 2020-2025.

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from pyprojroot import here
```

### Expand spending data to 2020-2025

```{python}
file_lawenf_2 = here("projects/wa-state-police-social-spending/_data/le_20-25.csv")
le_spending_2020_2025 = pd.read_csv(file_lawenf_2, skiprows=6)

file_social_2 = here("projects/wa-state-police-social-spending/_data/social_20-25.csv")
social_spending_2020_2025 = pd.read_csv(file_social_2, skiprows=6)
```

```{python}
#sort into only counties for law enforcement spending data
le_spending_2020_2025 = le_spending_2020_2025[le_spending_2020_2025["Governments/$ Dollars"].str.endswith("County", na=False)]

#39 counties total in WA
#len(le_spending_2020_2025) #output is 39!

#sorting into only counties for social services spending data
social_spending_2020_2025 = social_spending_2020_2025[social_spending_2020_2025["Governments/$ Dollars"].str.endswith("County", na=False)]

#39 counties total in WA
#len(social_spending_2020_2025) #output is 39!
```

```{python}
#cleaning dollar values in the spending data
for year in range(2020, 2026):
    col = str(year)
    le_spending_2020_2025[col] = (
        le_spending_2020_2025[col]
        .str.replace("$", "", regex=False)
        .str.replace(",", "", regex=False)
    )
    le_spending_2020_2025[col] = pd.to_numeric(
        le_spending_2020_2025[col], errors="coerce"
    ) #some unexpected values in the dollar column, so replacing these with NaN

#cleaning dollar values in the data
for year in range(2020, 2026):
    col = str(year)
    social_spending_2020_2025[col] = (
        social_spending_2020_2025[col]
        .str.replace("$", "", regex=False)
        .str.replace(",", "", regex=False)
    )
    social_spending_2020_2025[col] = pd.to_numeric(
        social_spending_2020_2025[col], errors="coerce"
    ) #some unexpected values in the dollar column, so replacing these with NaN
```

I also cleaned the dollar amounts in the spending data so that each observation would be classified as an integer/float and it would be possible to sum values together. Finally, there were some observations in the spending data that were listed as "No filing" or "Pending revision" as of November 23, 2026. In the 2024 data for both law enforcement and social services spending, there was one county that was pending revision. In the 2021 data, there was one county pending revision. In the 2025 data, there was one county pending revision and three counties with no filing. I handled this by assigning these observations as NaN. This ensured that these counties could be included in the dataset, but that missing values would not impede the analysis.

```{python}
#keep county and year columbs
years = [str(year) for year in range(2020, 2026)]

le_spending_2020_2025 = le_spending_2020_2025[["Governments/$ Dollars"] + years]
social_spending_2020_2025 = social_spending_2020_2025[["Governments/$ Dollars"] + years]

#rename county column
le_spending_2020_2025 = le_spending_2020_2025.rename(columns={
    "Governments/$ Dollars": "County"})

social_spending_2020_2025 = social_spending_2020_2025.rename(columns={
    "Governments/$ Dollars": "County"})

#cleaing county names
le_spending_2020_2025["County"] = le_spending_2020_2025["County"].str.replace(" County", "", regex=False)
social_spending_2020_2025["County"] = social_spending_2020_2025["County"].str.replace(" County", "", regex=False)

#reshaping because i want year as a column
le_spending_2020_2025 = le_spending_2020_2025.melt(
    id_vars="County",
    var_name="Year",
    value_name="Law Enforcement Spending")

social_spending_2020_2025 = social_spending_2020_2025.melt(
    id_vars="County",
    var_name="Year",
    value_name="Social Spending")

#merging both spending dfs
spending = le_spending_2020_2025.merge(
    social_spending_2020_2025,
    on=["County", "Year"])

#make year an integer
spending["Year"] = spending["Year"].astype(int)

#sorting by county & year
spending = spending.sort_values(["County", "Year"])
```

Column names were cleaned, and the law enforcement and social services spending data were joined into a single dataframe. This required reshaping for both dataframes, as years 2020-2025 needed to be in a single "Year" column rather than each their own column.

### Population
```{python}
#import population data
file_pop = here("projects/wa-state-police-social-spending/_data/populations.csv")
population = pd.read_csv(file_pop)

#cleaning county names
population["County"] = population["County"].str.removeprefix(".")
population["County"] = population["County"].str.replace(" County, Washington", "", regex=False)

#keeping just county and necessary year columns
years = [str(year) for year in range(2020, 2026)]
population = population[["County"] + years]

#reshaping
population = population.melt(
    id_vars="County",
    var_name="Year",
    value_name="Population")

#year: str -> int
population["Year"] = population["Year"].astype(int)

#lose commas in population and convert type
population["Population"] = (
    population["Population"]
    .astype(str)
    .str.replace(",", "", regex=False))

population["Population"] = pd.to_numeric(
    population["Population"], errors="coerce")

#merge w/ spending data
county_data = spending.merge(
    population,
    on=["County", "Year"],
    how="left",
    validate="one_to_one")

county_data.head()
```

### Crime

```{python}
file_crime_2020 = here("projects/wa-state-police-social-spending/_data/crime_2020.csv")
crime_2020 = pd.read_csv(file_crime_2020)
file_crime_2021 = here("projects/wa-state-police-social-spending/_data/crime_2021.csv")
crime_2021 = pd.read_csv(file_crime_2021)
file_crime_2022 = here("projects/wa-state-police-social-spending/_data/crime_2022.csv")
crime_2022 = pd.read_csv(file_crime_2022)
file_crime_2023 = here("projects/wa-state-police-social-spending/_data/crime_2023.csv")
crime_2023 = pd.read_csv(file_crime_2023)
file_crime_2024 = here("projects/wa-state-police-social-spending/_data/crime_2024.csv")
crime_2024 = pd.read_csv(file_crime_2024)
file_crime_2025 = here("projects/wa-state-police-social-spending/_data/crime_2025.csv")
crime_2025 = pd.read_csv(file_crime_2025)

#defining violent offenses
violent_offenses = [
    "Murder Non Negligent Manslaughter",
    "Rape",
    "Robbery",
    "Aggravated Assault"]

crime_dfs = [crime_2020, crime_2021, crime_2022,
    crime_2023, crime_2024, crime_2025]

crime_all = []

for year, df in zip(range(2020, 2026), crime_dfs):
    #removes State Agency which was listed as a county
    df = df[df["County"] != "State Agency"].copy()
    #remove caps lock
    df["County"] = df["County"].str.title()
    #classify offenses based on earlier definition
    df["Crime Type"] = np.where(
        df["Offense"].isin(violent_offenses),
        "Violent Offenses",
        "Other Offenses")
    county_crime = (
        df.groupby(["County", "Crime Type"])
        .size()
        .unstack(fill_value=0)
        .reindex(columns=["Violent Offenses", "Other Offenses"], fill_value=0)
        .reset_index())
    #calc total offenses
    county_crime["Total Offenses"] = (
        county_crime["Violent Offenses"] + county_crime["Other Offenses"])
    #adding year
    county_crime["Year"] = year
    crime_all.append(county_crime)

#combine all years
crime_all = pd.concat(crime_all, ignore_index=True)

crime_all.head()
```

### Join crime, spending, population

```{python}
#rm existing crime columns before merging
crime_cols = [
    "Violent Offenses",
    "Other Offenses",
    "Total Offenses"]

county_data = county_data.drop(
    columns=crime_cols + [f"{col}{suffix}" for col in crime_cols for suffix in ["_x", "_y"]],
    errors="ignore")

#merging crime data
county_data = county_data.merge(
    crime_all,
    on=["County", "Year"],
    how="left",
    validate="one_to_one")
```

```{python}
#adding per capita spending and offenses per 100k (crime rate)
#law enforcement spending pc
county_data["Law Enforcement Spending Per Capita"] = (
    county_data["Law Enforcement Spending"] / county_data["Population"])

#social spending pc
county_data["Social Spending Per Capita"] = (
    county_data["Social Spending"] / county_data["Population"])

#total offenses per 100k population
county_data["Offenses Per 100k (crime rate)"] = (
    county_data["Total Offenses"] / county_data["Population"] * 100000)

#violent offenses
county_data["Violent Offenses Per 100k (crime rate)"] = (
    county_data["Violent Offenses"] / county_data["Population"] * 100000)

#other offenses
county_data["Other Offenses Per 100k (crime rate)"] = (
    county_data["Other Offenses"] / county_data["Population"] * 100000)
```

## How have law enforcement spending, social spending, and crime changed over time?


## Do counties that increase police spending experience changes in violent crime?

```{python}
#select 2020 and 2025 data
change_20_25 = county_data[
    county_data["Year"].isin([2020, 2025])].copy()

change_20_25 = change_20_25.pivot(
    index="County",
    columns="Year",
    values=[
        "Law Enforcement Spending Per Capita",
        "Violent Offenses Per 100k (crime rate)",
        "Social Spending Per Capita"])

#calc changes 2020 -> 2025
change_20_25["Law Enforcement Spending Change"] = (
    change_20_25["Law Enforcement Spending Per Capita"][2025] -
    change_20_25["Law Enforcement Spending Per Capita"][2020])

#social spending
change_20_25["Social Spending Change"] = (
    change_20_25["Social Spending Per Capita"][2025] -
    change_20_25["Social Spending Per Capita"][2020])

change_20_25["Violent Crime Rate Change"] = (
    change_20_25["Violent Offenses Per 100k (crime rate)"][2025] -
    change_20_25["Violent Offenses Per 100k (crime rate)"][2020])

change_20_25 = change_20_25.reset_index()
```

```{python}
change_20_25
```

```{python}
#remove the NaNs
plot_1 = change_20_25[
    ["Law Enforcement Spending Change", "Violent Crime Rate Change"]].dropna()

x = plot_1["Law Enforcement Spending Change"]
y = plot_1["Violent Crime Rate Change"]

plt.scatter(x, y)

m, b = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)
plt.plot(x, m*x + b, color="red")

plt.axhline(0, color="gray", linestyle="--")
plt.axvline(0, color="gray", linestyle="--")

plt.xlabel("Change in Law Enforcement Spending Per Capita ($)")
plt.ylabel("Change in Violent Offenses per 100,000")
plt.title("1. Changes in Police Spending and Violent Crime (2020–2025)")
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#calc correlation
change_20_25["Law Enforcement Spending Change"].corr(
    change_20_25["Violent Crime Rate Change"])
```

Counties ounties with larger increases in law enforcement spending per capita tended to experience smaller increases, or larger decreases, in violent crime rates between 2020 and 2025.

## Do counties that increase social service spending experience changes in violent crime?

```{python}
#remove the NaNs
plot_2 = change_20_25[
    ["Social Spending Change", "Violent Crime Rate Change"]].dropna()

x = plot_2["Social Spending Change"]
y = plot_2["Violent Crime Rate Change"]

plt.scatter(x, y)

m, b = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)
plt.plot(x, m*x + b, color="red")

plt.axhline(0, color="gray", linestyle="--")
plt.axvline(0, color="gray", linestyle="--")

plt.xlabel("Change in Social Spending Per Capita ($)")
plt.ylabel("Change in Violent Offenses per 100,000")
plt.title("2. Changes in Social Spending and Violent Crime (2020–2025)")
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#calc correlation
change_20_25["Social Spending Change"].corr(
    change_20_25["Violent Crime Rate Change"])
```

Both law enforcement spending and social spending have a similar pattern. Between 2020 and 2025, changes in law enforcement spending and social service spending per capita were weakly negatively correlated with changes in violent crime rates. The correlation coefficient is -0.248 for law enforcement spending and -0.220 for social spending. The correlation results suggest that counties that experience larger increases in either spending category tend to experience smaller increases in violent crime. Importantly, neither relationship is very strong and the correlations alone cannot establish that increased spending of either kind led to reductions in crime.

## Follow up question: Are counties that are increasing law enforcement spending also increasing social spending?

```{python}
change_20_25["Law Enforcement Spending Change"].corr(
    change_20_25["Social Spending Change"])
```

The coefficient doesn't support the hypothesis that counties that increase law enforcement spending are also increasing social spending. Changes in both spending categories seem to be unrelated.

## Testing statistical significance

```{python}
#construct multiple linear regression model
model_data = change_20_25[
    ["Law Enforcement Spending Change",
     "Social Spending Change",
     "Violent Crime Rate Change"]].dropna()

model = smf.ols(
    'Q("Violent Crime Rate Change") ~ Q("Law Enforcement Spending Change") + Q("Social Spending Change")',
    data=model_data).fit()

print(model.summary())
```

The multiple linear regression model found negative coefficients for both spending categories. The estimated coefficient for law enforcement spending was −0.347 (p=0.139), and the coefficient for social spending was −0.256 (p=0.185). Neither relationship was statistically significant at the 5% level. The model can explain approximately 11.2% of the variation in violent crime rate changes across the 35 counties included in the analysis (4 counties were excluded due to missing values). These results don't provide sufficient evidence to establish statistically significant relationships betwee the variables.

## Are police spending and social spending increased proportionately?

```{python}
#look at 202 and 2025
spending_change = county_data[
    county_data["Year"].isin([2020, 2025])].copy()

spending_change = spending_change.pivot(
    index="County",
    columns="Year",
    values=[
        "Law Enforcement Spending Per Capita",
        "Social Spending Per Capita"])

#percent change in police
spending_change["Police Growth (%)"] = (
    (spending_change["Law Enforcement Spending Per Capita"][2025] -
     spending_change["Law Enforcement Spending Per Capita"][2020]) /
    spending_change["Law Enforcement Spending Per Capita"][2020]) * 100

#percent change in social
spending_change["Social Growth (%)"] = (
    (spending_change["Social Spending Per Capita"][2025] -
     spending_change["Social Spending Per Capita"][2020]) /
    spending_change["Social Spending Per Capita"][2020]) * 100

spending_change = spending_change.reset_index()
```

```{python}
#avg spending growth
print("Average police spending growth:",
      spending_change["Police Growth (%)"].mean())

print("Average social spending growth:",
      spending_change["Social Growth (%)"].mean())
```     

```{python}
#try median too
spending_change[
    ["Police Growth (%)", "Social Growth (%)"]].median()
```

Social spending grew more than law enforcement spending between 2020 and 2025. Both the average and median calculations for growth show this, so I'm confident that outliers are not skewing this finding.

```{python}
#visualization of spending growth
x = spending_change["Police Growth (%)"]
y = spending_change["Social Growth (%)"]

plt.scatter(x, y)

plt.axline((0, 0), slope=1, color="red", linestyle="--")

plt.xlabel("Police Spending Growth (%)")
plt.ylabel("Social Spending Growth (%)")
plt.title("3. Police vs. Social Spending Growth (2020–2025)")

plt.show()
```
